facts.title: AiFlow: Token-Native Reactive Orchestration with Bounded Backpressure for Streaming LLM Applications
facts.event_hint: AiFlow makes token-level LLM application events typed graph data with declarative bounded queues and backpressure
facts.problem: Streaming LLM workflows often expose provider deltas through callbacks while leaving queue capacity, worker allocation, ordering, cancellation, retry, and backpressure to ad hoc code. Aggregating a full response delays downstream work and unbounded queues can exhaust memory under slow consumers.
facts.mechanism: AiFlow normalizes provider deltas and control signals into typed Context<T> events on a directed graph. A Node Guardian owns each node's bounded input queue, worker budget, ordering buffer, cancellation and retry state, overflow policy, side-effect mode, and metrics. A DSL/JSON compiler validates edge types, cycles, state-concurrency, and injection compatibility before execution; token-level routing overlaps generation with downstream processing while backpressure propagates or applies declared overflow behavior.

evidence.claim: AiFlow does not change provider-side Model TTFT but reduces Application TTFPT by 70.9–94.7% versus aggregation across captured DeepSeek and local Ollama workloads.
evidence.baseline: aggregation that waits for the complete model response
evidence.condition: paired trace replay or local controlled replay; Model TTFT unchanged
evidence.source_locator: PDF p.1 abstract; p.17 Table 12; p.20 conclusion

evidence.claim: Compared with unbounded policies, declared bounded queues reduce MaxQ by 93.7–96.5% while preserving first-token latency.
evidence.condition: DeepSeek semantic routing, DeepSeek streaming RAG, and Ollama qwen2.5:3b

evidence.claim: In controlled semantic routing, Application TTFPT was 210±10 ms for AiFlow versus 10,940±60 ms for aggregation, while Model TTFT was 101±2 ms for both.
evidence.value: 210±10 ms vs 10,940±60 ms; Model TTFT 101±2 ms
evidence.condition: deterministic stream; 30 measured runs after 5 warmups

evidence.claim: With a slow TTS-like consumer taking 500 ms per token, AiFlow kept maximum queue depth at the declared bound of 8 with no drops or errors.
evidence.baseline: no-backpressure policy reached MaxQ=131 in the controlled ablation
evidence.condition: slow downstream consumer; queue capacity q=8

evidence.claim: In 30-run DeepSeek semantic-routing replay, AiFlow reduced Application TTFPT from 5,495.0±1,564.3 ms aggregation to 1,151.9±352.4 ms while limiting MaxQ to 8.0 instead of 231.2.

facts.evaluation_context: The paper separates provider Model TTFT from application-layer TTFPT. Controlled runs use a deterministic stream on a Java/OpenJDK 21 Linux CPU-only prototype with 5 warmups and 30 measured runs; captured DeepSeek replay uses 30 identical traces and paired statistical tests; online and LangGraph checks are descriptive.
facts.limitations: AiFlow is an application-layer orchestration model and does not optimize transformer serving, KV cache, GPU batching, provider scheduling, or remote provider buffers. The study does not measure distributed placement, provider multi-tenancy/GPU contention, long-running fault recovery, large-scale RAG quality, or adaptive runtime scheduling. Carefully configured async baselines approach its raw latency, so the primary contribution is declaration, validation, and bounded orchestration rather than a new primitive.
facts.project_relevance: AiFlow's typed events, declarative queue/worker policies, and evidence of bounded MaxQ map directly to tool-calling and streaming Agent pipelines. It suggests separating model TTFT from application TTFPT and enforcing task-specific backpressure/cancellation outside the model, while preserving ordering and auditing side effects.
source_notes: The arXiv v1 PDF and all three referenced chunks were fetched; evidence locators refer to PDF pages and tables.
Performance claims are stated with their baseline and paired/replay conditions; provider-side speedup is not inferred.
